title: Does India's 4-Day Work Week Actually Give You a Day Off?
meta_title: Does India's 4-Day Work Week Actually Give You a Day Off? | Aperture
summary: India legalized a 4-day work week in 2026, but total hours stay at 48. That means 12-hour days, not a shorter week. Here's who should and shouldn't opt in.

content:
India legalized a 4-day work week in May 2026, and yes, you do get an extra day off from the office. But not a shorter week. The total hours stay at 48, which means four 12-hour days instead of five shorter ones. A different shape for the same 48 hours.

Whether that trade is worth it depends on your commute, your role, and what your evenings look like. Some workers genuinely come out ahead. Others are signing up for longer Tuesdays in exchange for a Monday off.

Key Takeaways

  • India's 4-day week is a compressed schedule: 4 days at 12 hours each, totaling 48 hours. Hours don't shrink.
  • It's optional for both companies and employees. No employer is required to offer it, and workers must consent before it applies to them.
  • Long-distance commuters and output-measured roles, like IT and consulting work, are most likely to benefit.
  • Parents with school-age children, physically demanding jobs, and anyone already near burnout are better off on the standard schedule.
  • Global 4-day week pilots in the UK and Iceland cut total hours to 32 per week. India's version doesn't. These are two different things.

What India's New Labor Code Actually Changed

Under the rules notified in May 2026, employers can offer employees a compressed 4-day schedule where each working day is capped at 12 hours. The 48-hour weekly ceiling hasn't moved. No company is required to adopt the model, and employees must agree to it in writing before it applies.

Labor sits on India's Concurrent List, so states need to adopt the central rules before they take effect locally. Karnataka, Telangana, and Maharashtra are expected to move first because of their large IT workforces. Manufacturing-heavy states will likely follow a year or more later.

Overtime rules stay in place. Any hours worked beyond 12 in a day must be compensated at the applicable overtime rate. That ceiling isn't optional.

India's 4-Day Week vs the Global Model: A Comparison

Most of the global conversation around 4-day weeks is built on reducing hours, not rearranging them. India's model is different, and mixing them up leads to false expectations about what you're actually signing up for.

The UK and Iceland trials ran on a 100-80-100 model: 100 percent pay, 80 percent of hours, 100 percent of the expected output. India's version keeps hours intact and redistributes them. Both result in a 4-day schedule. The reasoning behind them is entirely different.

Who Actually Benefits From a Compressed 4-Day Schedule?

The workers who gain the most share one thing: their commute is the real drain, not the working hours. If you're spending 2 to 3 hours a day getting to and from an office in Bengaluru or Hyderabad, cutting that to 4 days saves a meaningful amount of weekly transit time. The longer working day becomes a fair trade when commute days drop by 20 percent.

Remote workers and consultants who already clock long hours on most days often find that the mental cost of starting up and shutting down each morning is higher than it seems. Building a concentrated daily rhythm is often the neccessary foundation for making compressed weeks work. Those who thrive under this model tend to front-load their hardest work and handle admin later in the day.

People who should think carefully before opting in:

  • Parents with school-age children. A 7 AM to 7 PM schedule doesn't align with school hours, and pickup gaps don't disappear because Monday is free.
  • Workers in physically demanding roles. Fatigue compounds after about 10 hours. A 12-hour shift is harder than one and a half normal shifts, not equivalent.
  • Roles requiring steady daily availability, like client support or cross-time-zone coordination. A Thursday off creates coverage gaps that fall on teammates.
  • Anyone already near burnout. Fewer days doesn't mean fewer hours, and 12-hour stretches intensify pressure that's already there.

What Indian Companies Are Actually Doing

The real list of Indian companies running a 4-day model is short. Springworks operates it as a standard offering. Zerodha and Beroe Inc. are among the other early movers. Infosys and HCL Technologies have joined government observation programs under the new rules but haven't announced company-wide adoption.

Most large employers are watching. The law permits the model but doesn't mandate it, and HR teams want attrition and output numbers from early movers before committing resources to a seperate scheduling infrastructure. That data is still thin.

If you want a compressed schedule at your current company, you'll probably have to ask for it rather than wait. The case is easier when your role tracks output, like software development or data work, and harder in roles defined by physical presence or fixed availability windows.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the 4-day work week mandatory for Indian companies?

No. The new labor code makes the compressed 4-day schedule legally permissible, not required. Companies decide whether to offer it, and employees must give written consent before the arrangement applies. No employer is obligated to adopt it, and no worker can be forced into 12-hour days without agreeing first.

Will my salary or PF contributions change under a 4-day schedule?

No. Since total weekly hours stay at 48, your salary, provident fund contributions, and gratuity calculations remain unchanged. The compressed schedule moves hours to fewer days without reducing them. You're not taking a pay cut, and PF deductions are calculated on the same basis as a standard 5-day schedule.

How is India's model different from the 4-day weeks trialed in the UK and Iceland?

The UK and Iceland trials cut total working hours to around 32 per week with full pay, based on evidence that output stayed steady. India's model keeps the 48-hour cap and distributes those hours across 4 days. Both call it a 4-day week. The actual amount of time worked is very different.

Can I ask my employer for a 4-day schedule even if they haven't offered it?

You can raise it. The law permits it, though companies aren't required to agree. Roles with clear output metrics, like software development, writing, or data analysis, are easier to build a case for than roles tied to fixed business hours, in-person requirements, or service availability windows.

What happens to overtime under the compressed schedule?

Any hours worked beyond 12 in a single day count as overtime and must be compensated at the applicable rate. The 48-hour weekly cap also applies: working more than 48 hours across the 4 days is overtime by standard calculation. The compressed schedule doesn't exempt an employer from overtime obligations.

Which states in India have adopted the new labor code rules?

As of mid-2026, rollout is uneven. Labor falls under India's Concurrent List, so each state adopts separately. Karnataka, Telangana, and Maharashtra are expected among the early movers given their large IT sectors. Manufacturing-heavy states are likely a year or more behind. Check your state's notified rules before assuming the option is available where you work.

The Short Version

India's 4-day work week is now legal. But it's a compressed schedule, not a shorter one. The hours don't change. You still work 48 per week, just over 4 long days instead of 5 medium ones.

Worth a conversation with your manager if your commute is brutal and your output is measurable. Skip it if neither applies.
